en: Now, therefore, we shall explain Dharma. That from which the attainment of prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) results is Dharma.
Because it is taught by him (the Veda), the scripture (*āmnāya*) possesses authority.

From the knowledge of the true nature of the categories—substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence—arising from the specific properties of *dharma*, through their similarities and differences, comes the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).
(KVs 1.1.4) Earth, water, fire, air, ether, time, space, self, and mind are the substances.

(KVs 1.1.5) Color, taste, smell, touch, numbers, dimensions, separateness, conjunction and disjunction, priority and posteriority, cognitions, pleasure and pain, desire and aversion, and efforts are the qualities. (KVs 1.1.6)
Throwing upward, throwing downward, contraction, expansion, and locomotion are the [five] actions (karmāṇi).

KVs_1,1.7 Existence, non-eternality, possessing substance, being an effect, being a cause, and possessing generality and particularity—these are the common characteristics (aviśeṣa) of substances, qualities, and actions.
KVs_1,1.8 The similarity (sādharmya) between substances and qualities is their capacity to originate [effects] of their own kind. KVs_1,1.9
Substances originate another substance, and qualities originate another quality.
(KVs 1.1.10) Action is not found to be produced by action.
(KVs 1.1.11) A substance does not become a cause [of another substance]. (KVs 1.1.12)
Qualities exist in both ways [as causes and as effects].
(KVs 1.1.13) Action is that which is opposed to its own effect.
(KVs 1.1.14) "Substance is that which possesses action and qualities and is an inherent cause"—this is the definition of substance. (KVs 1.1.15)
"Subsisting in a substance, possessing qualities, and being non-causal and independent with respect to conjunctions and disjunctions"—this is the definition of a quality (guṇa). KVs 1.1.16.
"Residing in a single substance, devoid of qualities, and being an independent cause with respect to conjunctions and disjunctions"—this is the definition of action (karman). KVs 1.1.17.
"With respect to substances, qualities, and actions, substance is the common cause. KVs 1.1.18.
Likewise, quality [is the common property].
Action is common to conjunction, disjunction, and speed;
it is not common to substances.
Because of its exclusion [from the category of substance].
(KVs 1.1.22) Substance is the effect of substances, as it is their universal. (KVs 1.1.23) Action is not the effect of actions, because of the dissimilarity of qualities. (KVs 1.1.24)
Numbers beginning with duality, as well as separateness, conjunction, and disjunction [do not have action as their non-inherent cause].
(KVs 1.1.25) Because they are not inherent causes, action does not exist as a product of generality. (KVs 1.1.26) Substance is the effect of conjunctions. (KVs 1.1.27)
The color-form of color-forms;
upward motion resulting from gravity, effort, and conjunction;
and conjunctions and disjunctions result from actions.

In the general case of causes, it has been stated that among substances and actions, action is not a cause [of another action]. (KVs 1.1.31) From the absence of a cause follows the absence of the effect;
however, from the absence of the effect, there is no absence of the cause. (KVs 1.2.1–2)
"Universal and particular" is dependent upon cognition.

(KVs 1.2.3) Being (*bhāva*) is only a universal because it is the cause of inclusive application (*anuvṛtti*) alone. (KVs 1.2.4) Substantiality (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), and action-ness (*karmatva*) are both universals and particulars. (KVs 1.2.5)
Except for the ultimate particularities (antyaviśeṣas).
(KVs 1.2.6) That from which [the cognition] "existent" arises with respect to substances, qualities, and actions is Being (sattā).
(KVs 1.2.7) Being is a distinct entity from substances, qualities, and actions. (KVs 1.2.8)
And because it exists in qualities and actions, it is neither an action nor a quality (KVs 1.2.9).
And because of the absence of particular universals, [it is not a universal] (KVs 1.2.10).
Its status as a substance has been stated due to its possessing multiple substances (KVs 1.2.11).
And because of the absence of generalities and particularities;
likewise, "quality-ness" (guṇatva) is stated [to exist] in qualities because of their presence there,
and because of the absence of generalities and particularities.
The state of being an action (*karmatva*) has been stated because [the word *karman*] occurs in the sense of actions;
and also because there is no distinction between a general property and a particular.
(KVs 1.2.15–16) Because the gender [of the term *sat*] is non-distinctive and because there is an absence of specific gender markers, existence (*bhāva*) is one. (KVs 1.2.17)
Earth possesses color, taste, smell, and tangibility.
Water possesses color, taste, and tangibility; it is fluid and cohesive.
Fire possesses color and tangibility.
Air possesses tangibility;
these [qualities] do not exist in space.
The liquidity of clarified butter, lac, and beeswax, due to contact with fire, shares a commonality with water.
The state of liquefaction resulting from contact with fire in tin, lead, iron, silver, and gold is a commonality shared with water.
(KVs 2.1.7) Having horns, possessing a hump, having a tail-tip, and having a dewlap are observed as marks for the nature of a cow. (KVs 2.1.8) And touch is the mark of wind. (KVs 2.1.9)
And because there is no contact with [the wind] when it is not seen, air has an unperceived mark (liṅga).
It is a substance by virtue of its lack of being a quality-possessor (adravyavattva). It is a substance also by virtue of possessing action and possessing qualities.
Eternity has been stated [to belong] to that which lacks substance (adravyatva).
(KVs 2.1.13) The convergence of winds is a mark of their plurality.
(KVs 2.1.14) Because there is no perception when wind is in contact [with the senses], no visible mark exists. (KVs 2.1.15)
And there is no distinction from the "inference based on general observation" (sāmānyato dṛṣṭa).
Therefore, it is based on scripture (āgamika).
However, the act of naming is a mark of those superior to us.
Because the act of naming proceeds from direct perception,
"going out" and "entering" are the marks of space. That [act] is not a mark [of space], because action possesses only a single substance.
And because of the non-inclusion of other causes and because of dissimilarity:
"The destruction of action [occurs] due to conjunction" (KVs 2.1.23).
"It is observed that the quality of an effect is preceded by the qualities of its cause" (KVs 2.1.24).
And because other effects do not arise [from it], sound is not a quality of tangible substances (KVs 2.1.25).
Because it inheres in something else and because it is perceptible, it is neither a quality of the self nor a quality of the mind (KVs 2.1.26).
By elimination, it is the inferential mark of space (KVs 2.1.27).
Substantiality and permanence are explained by [the case of] air (KVs 2.1.28). Its reality is established through its existence as a substance (KVs 2.1.29),
because there is no specific mark for sound and because there is an absence of any specific mark [to distinguish it otherwise] (KVs 2.1.30).

"And there is a single separateness due to following after that" (KVs 2.1.31). When there is contact between a flower and a cloth, the non-appearance of another quality [in the cloth] is the mark of the absence of odor in the cloth (KVs 2.2.1). Odor is restricted to earth (KVs 2.2.2).
By this, heat is explained:
[it is] the heat of fire (KVs 2.2.3);
[it is] the coldness in water (KVs 2.2.4–5).
"Posterior," "prior," "simultaneous," "long duration," and "quick"—these are the marks of time (kāla).
Its substantiality (dravyatva) and permanence (nityatva) are explained by [the discussion of] air (vāyu). Its reality (tattva) is through its mode of being (bhāva).
Because of its non-existence in eternal things and its existence in non-eternal things, [the quality] called time (kāla) resides in the cause.
(KVs 2.2.9) That from which one perceives "this is from here" is the indicative mark (liṅga) of direction (diś).
(KVs 2.2.10) Its substantiality (dravyatva) and eternality (nityatva) are explained by [the discussion of] wind (vāyu). (KVs 2.2.11)
By way of its essential nature [it is one];
by way of its specific effects, there is diversity.
Due to conjunction with the sun—whether past, future, or present—the term "eastern" [is applied].
Likewise, [the directions] south, west, and north.
By this, the intermediate directions are explained.
Doubt arises from the perception of a general property and the recollection of specific particulars.
And what is seen is treated as having been seen (KVs 2.2.18);
because of being seen as it was and not being seen as it was (KVs 2.2.19);
and because of knowledge and ignorance, there is doubt (KVs 2.2.20).

That object which is apprehended by the sense of hearing is sound (śabda). (KVs 2.2.21) Because a specific characteristic is observed in two ways—among things of the same class and among things belonging to different classes—it [is not a substance].
(KVs 2.2.22) It is not a substance because it does not reside in a single substance. (KVs 2.2.23)
Nor is it action, because it is not visible (KVs 2.2.24).
The cessation of an existing quality has a commonality with actions (KVs 2.2.25),
because there is no mark of its existence [prior to that cessation] (KVs 2.2.26).
Because of its constant dissimilarity [to space].
(KVs 2.2.27) And this [sound] is impermanent because it has a cause. (KVs 2.2.28) Nor is this [reason] unestablished, because of its modification. (KVs 2.2.29)
Because there is a fault in [the theory of] manifestation.
(KVs 2.2.30) Sound is produced from conjunction, from disjunction, and from sound. (KVs 2.2.31) Furthermore, sound is non-eternal because of its inferential mark. (KVs 2.2.32)
Because there is an absence of two [simultaneous] operations;
because of the word "first" (prathama);
and because of the existence of mutual agreement.
When there is plurality, they are doubtful;
[therefore] there is an absence of number in a general sense.
The objects of the senses are well-known.

The non-establishment of the sense-faculties and their objects is the reason for [the existence of] something distinct from the sense-faculties and their objects. (KVs 3.1.2) That is not a valid probans (anapadeśa). (KVs 3.1.3) Because there is no knowledge of the cause. (KVs 3.1.4)
Because of knowledge regarding the effect [it is a reason];
because of ignorance [regarding it, it is not].
That which is something else entirely from the reason is "non-indication" (anapadeśa).
For one thing is not the indicator of another thing.

[KVs 3.1.8] It is that which is conjoined, that which is inherent, that which inheres in the same object, and that which is contradictory. [KVs 3.1.9] An effect is [the indicator] of another effect. [KVs 3.1.10]
The non-existent is the contradictory of the existent; KVs 3.1.11. The existent is the contradictory of the non-existent; KVs 3.1.12. The existent is the contradictory of the existent; KVs 3.1.13.

Because a formal argument (*apadeśa*) is preceded by what is already established. That which is unestablished (*aprasiddha*) is not a formal argument; that which is non-existent (*asan*) and that which is doubtful (*sandigdha*) are also not formal arguments.
"Because it has horns, therefore it is a horse. (KVs 3.1.14–16)
"Because it has horns, therefore it is a cow"—this is an example of the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) [reason].

(KVs 3.1.17) "That which is produced from the contact of the self, the sense organs, and the objects is something else [than the body]" (KVs 3.1.18). "And activity and cessation, being observed in one's own self, are the mark (*liṅga*) for [the existence of] another. (KVs 3.1.19)
The existence and non-existence of cognition arising from the contact of the self, the sense organs, and their objects are the marks of the mind (manas).
Its status as a substance and its eternity are explained by [the discussion of] air. It is one, because of the non-simultaneity of effort and the non-simultaneity of cognitions.

Inhalation and exhalation, the opening and closing of the eyes, life, the movements of the mind, the modifications of the other sense organs, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort are the marks (liṅgas) of the self (ātman).
Its status as a substance and its eternity have been explained by [the discussion of] air.
Since there is no perception of it in proximity—as in the case of [saying] "Yajñadatta"—no perceived mark exists [for the self].

And there is no distinction from the "inference based on general observation" (sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa); therefore, it is based on scripture (āgamika). Because of the exclusion [of the word] "I," it is not based on scripture.
If it is perceived directly that "I am Devadatta" or "I am Yajñadatta," then,
because the sign (liṅga) in the self is seen as a single entity with firmness, the cognition is like a perception (pratyakṣavat).
The cognition regarding the body— such as "Devadatta goes" or "Yajñadatta goes"— is [actually] a metaphorical designation (upacāra).
But these figurative designations are doubtful.
(KVs 3.2.13) Because the notion "I" exists with respect to the internal self and does not exist with respect to anything else, it is a perception of a distinct entity.
(KVs 3.2.14) In the case of the expression "Devadatta goes," since it is based on figurative usage and [false] conceit, the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) is a perception of the body. (KVs 3.2.15)
But the metaphorical application is doubtful.

(KVs 3.2.16) However, [the self] is not the object of knowledge for Yajñadatta or Viṣṇumitra based on a particular body and so forth. (KVs 3.2.17) Because the distinction [of the self] is established through the non-deviation of its absence [from the body], just as in the case of words [denoting the self] used in their primary or secondary senses in the expression "I," it is not based on scripture. (KVs 3.2.18)
The self is one because there is no distinction in the production of pleasure, pain, and cognition;
it is manifold because of the established order [of experience];
and also by the authority of the scriptures.
That which possesses the nature of having no cause is eternal. (KVs 4.1.1) Its effect is its mark.
(KVs 4.1.2) From the absence of a cause follows the absence of an effect. (KVs 4.1.3)
"Impermanent" is the state of specific negation (KVs 4.1.4).
Ignorance (avidyā) (KVs 4.1.5).
Perception [of the great] occurs because it consists of multiple substances and possesses color/form (rūpa) (KVs 4.1.6).
Even though air possesses substantiality and magnitude, it is not perceived due to the absence of the manifestation of color (*rūpa*).
(KVs 4.1.7) The perception of color occurs because of its inherence in multiple substances and due to a specific quality of color.
(KVs 4.1.8) By this, the cognition of taste, odor, and touch is explained. (KVs 4.1.9)
Because of its absence, there is no deviation [from the rule].

(KVs 4.1.10) Numbers, dimensions, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, and action are visible by sight due to their inherence in substances that possess color. (KVs 4.1.11) In those [substances] lacking color, they are not visible by sight. (KVs 4.1.12)

By this, cognition through all the sense organs regarding quality (*guṇa*) and existence (*bhāva*) has been explained. Furthermore, that effect-substance consisting of earth and the other elements is threefold, being designated as body (*śarīra*), sense organ (*indriya*), and object (*viṣaya*).
Because the conjunction of things that are both perceptible and imperceptible is itself imperceptible, there is no [body] composed of five elements.
And because no other qualities arise, it is not composed of the three [guṇas]. However, the conjunction of atoms is not prohibited.
In that regard, the body is of two kinds: born from a womb and not born from a womb.
Because they are not preceded by a fixed direction or location;
because of the distinction of their specific qualities;
and because of the absence of a conventional designation.
Because it is the first among the [mental] formations (saṃjñā);
because there are those born not from a womb;
and because of the evidence found in the Vedas.
Action in the hand arises from the conjunction of the self and effort (KVs 5.1.1).
Likewise, action in the pestle arises from conjunction with the hand (KVs 5.1.2).
In the case of action produced by impact in the pestle and so forth, conjunction with the hand is not the cause due to its absence [when the impact occurs independently] (KVs 5.1.3).
Likewise, in the case of the action of the hand, there is conjunction with the self.
(KVs 5.1.4) From impact—that is, from conjunction with a pestle—there is action in the hand.
(KVs 5.1.5) And [action arises] from conjunction with the hand due to the action of the self. (KVs 5.1.6)
In the absence of conjunction, falling occurs due to gravity.
(KVs 5.1.7) Due to the absence of a specific impulse, there is no upward or horizontal motion. (KVs 5.1.8) A specific impulse arises from a specific effort. (KVs 5.1.9)
From a particular kind of pushing arises a particular kind of throwing upward.
By the action of the hand, the action of the child is explained.
Likewise [is explained] the bursting of that which is burnt.
In the absence of effort, there is the movement of one who is asleep;
(KVs 5.1.13) the movement of grass is due to contact with the wind; (KVs 5.1.14) and the movement of a gem or the gliding of a needle has the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) as its cause. (KVs 5.1.15)

The various specific conjunctions occurring at non-simultaneous intervals are the cause for the diversity of actions in an arrow. (KVs 5.1.16) The first action of the arrow arises from the impulsion; from the momentum produced by that action, the subsequent [action] occurs, and likewise each succeeding one.
(KVs 5.1.17) In the absence of momentum, falling occurs due to gravity. (KVs 5.1.18)
Action in earth arises from pushing, striking, and conjunction with that which is conjoined [to it].
That [action] is produced by the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) due to its specific nature.
In the case of water, falling occurs due to gravity when there is an absence of conjunction [with another substance].
Flowing occurs due to fluidity (KVs_5,2.4).
Ascent through the stalk occurs due to contact with air (KVs_5,2.5),
as well as from impulsion, compression, and contact-with-the-contacted (saṃyuktasaṃyoga) (KVs_5,2.6).
The climbing of trees is caused by the unseen force (adṛṣṭa). The solidification and liquefaction of water result from contact with fire.
In this regard, thunder is the indicative mark.
And there is that which is Vedic:
"From the conjunction and from the disjunction of waters comes the sound of thunder" (KVs 5.2.10).
By the action of the earth, the action of fire and the action of air are explained (KVs 5.2.11–12).
The upward flaming of fire, the horizontal movement of air, and the initial action of atoms and of the mind are caused by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).
The action of the mind is explained by [the analogy of] the action of the hand. Pleasure and pain arise from the contact of the self, the sense organs, the mind, and their objects.

When the mind is established in the Self, there is no further activity [of the body]; that absence of suffering in the body is liberation (*mokṣa*). (KVs 5.2.16) Departing, approaching, the conjunction with what is eaten and drunk, and conjunctions with other effects—these are caused by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). (KVs 5.2.17) In the absence of that [unseen force], there is an absence of conjunction and the non-manifestation [of the body]; this is liberation. (KVs 5.2.18)
Darkness is non-existence (abhāva), because it differs from the production of substance, quality, and action;
and because it is the obstruction of light by another substance. Space, time, and ether are devoid of action, because they differ from that which possesses action.
By this, actions and qualities are also explained.
(KVs 5.2.22) The inherence of those that are inactive is excluded by [the discussion of] actions.
(KVs 5.2.23) However, qualities are the non-inherent causes. (KVs 5.2.24)
Space is explained by means of qualities;
time, by means of its cause;
and the composition of sentences in the Veda is preceded by intelligence.
In the case of a Brahmin, the act of naming is a sign of success; KVs_6,1.2. Giving preceded by conscious intent [is a sign]; KVs_6,1.3.
Likewise, receiving [is a sign]; KVs_6,1.4.
Because the qualities of one self are not the cause for another self;
[this principle] does not apply in the case of eating contaminated food;
for "contaminated" refers to [food involving] injury.
From its co-utterance, there is a fault; [that fault] does not exist when it is not defective. Furthermore, there is the application [of the rule] to that which is qualified.
Or, there is engagement with what is equal or inferior.
By this, the taking of another's property from those who are righteous—whether they be inferior, equal, or superior—is explained. Likewise, there is the abandonment of those who are hostile.
If the other is inferior, one should sacrifice oneself; KVs_6,1.14.
If they are equal, one may sacrifice oneself or sacrifice the other; KVs_6,1.15.
If the other is superior, one should sacrifice oneself; KVs_6,1.16.
Among actions that have both seen and unseen purposes, when there is an absence of a seen purpose, the purpose is for the sake of spiritual prosperity (*abhyudaya*).

(KVs 6.2.1) Consecration, fasting, celibacy, residence in the teacher’s house, forest-dwelling, sacrifice, giving, sprinkling, and the observances regarding direction, lunar mansions, mantras, and time are for the sake of the unseen. (KVs 6.2.2) The four stages of life (*cāturāśramya*) consist of both those with defects (*upadhā*) and those without defects (*anupadhā*). (KVs 6.2.3)
Defilement by nature (*bhāvadoṣa*), defilement by contact (*upadhādoṣa*), and non-contact (*anupadhā*).
That which possesses desirable form, taste, smell, and touch, and has been sprinkled and consecrated with water, is pure (*śuci*). "Impure" (*aśuci*) is the negation of purity.
And there is a difference in meaning.

(KVs 6.2.7) For one who is not self-restrained, spiritual excellence does not arise from eating pure food because of the absence of a restrictive rule; or rather, it does arise because the restrictive rule is a distinct factor.
(KVs 6.2.8) And because [excellence] is absent when that [rule] is non-existent. (KVs 6.2.9)
Attachment arises from pleasure (KVs 6.2.10);
because of being composed of that [pleasure] (KVs 6.2.11);
and because of the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) (KVs 6.2.12).

And because of the distinction of genus. (KVs 6.2.13) Activity consisting of merit and demerit is preceded by desire and aversion. (KVs 6.2.14) Their conjunction and disjunction [are also preceded by them]. (KVs 6.2.15)
Liberation regarding one's own actions has been explained [in Chapter 6]. The qualities have been stated [in Chapter 7, verse 1.1]:
earth and the other elements, as well as color, taste, smell, and touch, are impermanent because the substances they inhere in are impermanent. [KVs 7,1.2]

By this, the eternality [of number] in eternal [substances] has been stated. (KVs 7.1.3) In water, fire, and air, it is eternal because the substance is eternal. (KVs 7.1.4) In non-eternal [substances], it is non-eternal because the substance is non-eternal. (KVs 7.1.5)

In the case of earth, qualities produced by heating (*pākaja*) are preceded by the qualities of their causes. (KVs 7.1.6) Because they reside in a single substance. (KVs 7.1.7) The perception and non-perception of the minute and the large have been explained in relation to eternal [substances]. (KVs 7.1.8)
And because of the multiplicity of causes. (KVs 7.1.9) Therefore, the atom is the opposite.
(KVs 7.1.10) [The distinction] "atom" and "large" exists because of the presence of specific qualities in that [object] and the absence of them in the other. (KVs 7.1.11)
Because they exist at the same time;
because of the illustrative example;
and the absence of atomicity and magnitude in [the categories of] atomicity and magnitude is explained by [the analysis of] action and quality.
Actions are explained by means of actions, and qualities by means of qualities (KVs 7.1.15).
Actions and qualities are also explained by means of minuteness and magnitude (KVs 7.1.16).
By this, length and shortness are explained (KVs 7.1.17).
In the impermanent, it is impermanent;
in the permanent, it is permanent;
the spherical is eternal.
And ignorance is the mark of knowledge.
(KVs 7.1.21) Space is great because of its pervasiveness, and so too is the self.
(KVs 7.1.22) Because it lacks that [pervasiveness], the mind is atomic. (KVs 7.1.23)
The directions are designated by their qualities (guṇa);
time is designated by its cause (kāraṇa).
Unity is a distinct entity (arthāntara) because it is different from color, taste, smell, and touch.
Likewise for separateness (*pṛthaktva*). (KVs 7.2.2) The absence of oneness and separateness in oneness and separateness is explained by [the analysis of] minuteness and magnitude.
(KVs 7.2.3) Because action and quality lack number, a universal oneness does not exist. (KVs 7.2.4)
That is erroneous.
Because there is no identity [between cause and effect], figurative designation (bhakti) does not exist.
Since there is neither identity nor distinctness between cause and effect, neither identity nor distinctness exists.
This has been explained regarding the two impermanent [substances].
(KVs 7.2.8) Conjunction is that which is produced by the action of one, that produced by the action of both, and that produced by another conjunction.
(KVs 7.2.9) By this, disjunction is also explained. (KVs 7.2.10)
The absence of conjunction and disjunction in conjunction and disjunction themselves is explained by [the same reasoning applied to] atomicity and magnitude (KVs 7.2.11).
Actions [are devoid of] actions, and qualities [are devoid of] qualities, by virtue of atomicity and magnitude (KVs 7.2.12).
Because there is no separate establishment (*yutasiddhi*) between cause and effect, conjunction and disjunction do not exist [between them] (KVs 7.2.13).
Because it is a quality (guṇa); KVs_7,2.14. A quality is also perceived; KVs_7,2.15.
Because it is devoid of action (niṣkriya); KVs_7,2.16.

Because of the application [of the terms] "existent" and "non-existent," [it follows that] the word and its object are unrelated (KVs 7.2.17). [This is so] because [the cognition arises] from a staff which is in conjunction [with a person], and from a particularity which is inherent [in it] (KVs 7.2.19).
The cognition of meaning from a word is conventional (sāmayika).
[The notions of] "far" and "near" arise from two things situated in the same direction and at the same time, which are respectively remote and proximate;
these arise from the priority of the cause and the posteriority of the cause.
The absence of priority and posteriority in priority and posteriority is explained by [the same reasoning as] smallness and largeness. Actions [are non-existent] in actions;
qualities [are non-existent] in qualities. (KVs 7.2.23–25)
That from which [the cognition] "this is here" arises with respect to cause and effect is inherence (*samavāya*).
[This is established] by way of its essential nature.
Knowledge regarding substances has been explained.
In that regard, the self and the mind are not perceptible. (KVs 8.1.2) In the exposition of cognition, the procedure for the production of cognition has been stated.
(KVs 8.1.3) When qualities and actions are in contact [with the senses], substance is the cause of the production of cognition. (KVs 8.1.4)
In the case of generalities and particulars, because there is an absence of further generalities and particulars, that [cognition] itself is the knowledge [of them].
(KVs 8.1.5) [The cognition] regarding substances, qualities, and actions depends upon generalities and particulars.
(KVs 8.1.6) Regarding a substance, [the cognition] depends upon substances, qualities, and actions. (KVs 8.1.7)

Because qualities and actions lack [other] qualities and actions, there is no dependence upon qualities and actions [in their cognition]. (KVs 8.1.8) From the whiteness inherent [in the substance] and from the cognition of whiteness, the cognition of the white [substance] arises; these two stand in the relation of cause and effect.
(KVs 8.1.9) In the case of substances, however, they are not causes for one another. (KVs 8.1.10)

The sequence of cognitions such as "pot" and "cloth" arises from the non-simultaneity of causes and the succession of causes, not from a causal relationship [between the cognitions themselves]. (KVs 8.1.11) Expressions such as "This is he," "It was done by you," and "Feed him" depend upon cognition.
(KVs 8.2.1) [The existence of the effect] occurs when [the cause] is perceived and does not occur when it is not perceived. (KVs 8.2.2)
The term *artha* refers to substances (*dravya*), qualities (*guṇa*), and actions (*karman*). (KVs 8.2.3) Among substances, the state of being composed of five elements is denied.
(KVs 8.2.4) Due to its predominance and its possession of odor, earth is the primary cause (*prakṛti*) in the cognition of odor. (KVs 8.2.5)
Likewise, water, fire, and air [are non-existent] prior [to their manifestation], because there is no distinction in taste, form, or touch,
and because of the absence of designation through action and quality. [It is] existent and non-existent.

Because non-existence lacks action, quality, and designation, it is a different entity [from existence]. (KVs 9.1.3) That which is existent is also non-existent. (KVs 9.1.4) And that which is other than this non-existence is non-existent. (KVs 9.1.5)
"Non-existent" [is known] because there is no perception of the thing as it actually is, just as there is a perception of its opposite despite the memory of the thing;
likewise, because there is a perception of existence when that [non-existence] is present.
By this, "non-pot," "non-cow," and "non-dharma" are explained.
"Non-existent" (abhūtam) and "does not exist" (nāsti) are not different in meaning.
"There is no jar in the house" is a negation of the connection between an existing jar and the house.
Through the conjunction of the self and the mind within the self, there is perception of the self.

Likewise, there is perception of other substances [by those whose internal organs are not concentrated]. (KVs 9.1.12) And for those who have withdrawn their concentration but whose internal organs are not yet concentrated, [there is perception] of actions and qualities due to their inherence in that [substance]. (KVs 9.1.13–14)
[Inference] regarding the qualities of the self arises from their inherence in the self.

(KVs 9.1.15) "‘This is the effect of that,’ ‘this is the cause of that,’ ‘this is conjoined with that,’ ‘this is opposed to that,’ and ‘this is inherent in that’—such is inference based on a mark. (KVs 9.2.1) "This is the effect of that," and "the relation between cause and effect," arise from the members [of the syllogism]. (KVs 9.2.2)
By this, verbal [inference] is explained.

(KVs 9.2.3) "Reason" (*hetu*), "indication" (*apadeśa*), "mark" (*liṅga*), "means of knowledge" (*pramāṇa*), and "instrument" (*karaṇa*) are not different in meaning. (KVs 9.2.4) This is because they depend upon the cognition that "this belongs to that. (KVs 9.2.5)
Memory arises from a particular conjunction of the self and from mental impressions (*saṃskāra*);
likewise do dreams and dream-vision (*svapnāntika*).
And from the [nature of] phenomena;
ignorance arises from defects of the sense faculties and from defects of mental impressions. That is corrupted cognition.
Knowledge is that which is not defective (KVs 9.2.12).
That which is revealed by the ṛṣis and the vision of the perfected ones arise from the [authoritative] teachings (dharma) (KVs 9.2.13).
Because of the distinction between the causes of the desired and the undesired, and because of their mutual opposition, pleasure and pain are distinct entities (KVs 10.1.1).
The absence of any interval between doubt and its resolution is the reason for their being distinct types of cognition.
Their accomplishment occurs through perception and inference.
[This applies] even to the thought, "It was."
And because the effect is not observed [in the whole] despite its existence;

because it is observed in other causes that are inherent in the same object; and because it exists in a single part—namely, in one [body] consisting of the head, back, belly, vital organs, and their specific parts, [the whole is inferred] from those specific parts.
It is called "cause" (kāraṇa) because of the inherence of the effect in the substance (KVs_10.2.1),
or because of conjunction (saṃyoga) [with it] (KVs_10.2.2);
actions [are so called] because of their inherence in the cause (KVs_10.2.3).
Likewise, in the case of color (*rūpa*), [the inherence of the universal "color-ness" occurs] due to inherence in the same object as its cause (KVs 10.2.4).
Conjunction belongs to the cloth due to inherence in its cause (KVs 10.2.5),
and also due to inherence in both the cause and the non-cause (KVs 10.2.6).
From the inherence in that which is conjoined [with fire], there arises the specific quality of fire.
(KVs 10.2.7) The performance of those things seen to have visible purposes, when no visible purpose is present, leads to spiritual prosperity.
(KVs 10.2.8) Because of that statement, the Veda is authoritative. (KVs 10.2.9)
